Bridget Dudley Edwards (1871– 27 October 1956), was an Irish suffragette and a member of Cumann na mBan in  Dublin.
Background
Her granddaughter Ruth Dudley Edwards is known for being an Irish Unionist, a historian, and a columnist for the Irish Sunday Independent. In describing her grandmother, Ruth said her "enthusiasms included at various times suffragism, ethicism, Anglophobia, nationalism, revolution, fascism and – until her death in the late 1950s – the illegal IRA." Bridget's son, Robert Dudley Edwards was an Irish historian.
Early life
While living in London, Bridget met her husband Walter Edwards, a civil servant born in Worcestershire England. Upon meeting, Walter was already married. After separating from his wife, they lived together in Dublin. Although unorthodox at the time, the were not married.
Irish suffrage
Bridget has been described as a "prominent" member of the Dublin Women's Suffrage Association. Her son stated how his mother kept a 'Votes for Women' banner on her children's pram.
Cumann na mBan
Following a split in support after John Redmond's appeal for Irish Volunteer members to enlist themselves in the British Army, some branches of Cumann na mBan remained affiliated to Redmond's later National Volunteers. Although fleeting, Bridget Dudley Edwards was directly responsible in setting up a related branch called the Women's National Council in 1915.
